vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to change something so that it fits one client instead of all of them
one specific situation in which a client actually uses the product
the person inside the client who argues for you when you are not in the room
the share of clients who leave over a period
how much of a market, or how many countries, a company is present in
a group of clients who are similar enough to be sold to the same way
a client who agrees to talk to another client about working with you
the point at which a problem stops being tolerable and somebody acts

paras: Ask a commercial team who their best client is and you will get a name. Ask why, and the room goes quiet. This is not a small problem. A company that cannot describe its best client in one sentence is a company that cannot find the next one, and most of the money spent looking for growth is spent because that sentence does not exist.

The sentence has a shape. It names a segment, which is a group of clients similar enough to be sold to the same way, and then it adds the two or three things that are actually true of the good ones and not of the others. Groups of over two thousand people, whose finance team already has an internal auditor, in countries where the filing is monthly. Those clauses are doing real work: each one removes half the market. What is left is small, specific and findable, which is the opposite of the list most companies are working from.

There is a second sentence and it is harder. It describes the person, not the company. The champion, who is the one who argues for you when nobody from your side is in the room, is almost never the person who signs. They are usually one level below, they have been embarrassed by the current system at least once, and they have a use case they can describe from memory. Companies that know how to describe that person tailor everything to them and win accounts nobody expected. Companies that do not describe anybody send the same deck to everybody, and then explain the churn as a market problem.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: Our best clients are large groups, whose finance teams already have an internal auditor.
The champion, who is rarely the person who signs, is usually one level below.
This works best in countries where the filing is monthly.
The use case we lead with is the audit, which is where their pain threshold is.
Mr Chen, whose team runs the pilot, is the one to send the plan to.
We tailor the deck to one person, and we say who that person is.

listenings.text: We spent about two years selling to everybody and calling it a strategy. The exercise that changed it took an afternoon. Somebody put our twenty best accounts on a wall and asked what they had in common, and the first three answers were useless. Big. Multinational. Complex. Then somebody said, their finance teams all have an internal auditor, and the room went quiet, because that was true of nineteen of the twenty and it was true of almost nobody we had been calling. From that afternoon we stopped describing our clients by size and started describing them by who was sitting in their finance team. Our pipeline got smaller and the close rate roughly doubled. And the uncomfortable part is that the information had been in the building the whole time. Nobody had ever written the sentence.

The person who signs is not the person you are selling to, and I wish somebody had told me that ten years earlier. The person who signs wants the risk explained in two lines. The person who actually decides is usually one level down, and she is the one who has lived with the old system, and she has a story about the week it failed. That person is your champion, whether you have identified her or not, and she is arguing your case in rooms you will never be in. So the question I ask now, in every first meeting, is: who else is going to be affected by this, and what happened to them last year? It sounds like small talk and it is the most commercial question in the conversation.
